alt: One float goes through two lines. round with two places gives back a float, which prints without any added trailing zero. The f-string spec dot 2 f gives back text with exactly two decimals. The table shows what each line gives and what it prints.

steps.caption: `x = float(input())` reads 3.1. Both lines below start from this one value.
`round(x, 2)` returns a float rounded to 2 places, 3.1. A float has no memory of how many digits you wanted, so `print` shows 3.1.
`f"{x:.2f}"` returns text with exactly 2 digits after the point: 3.10. It is a string, so the digits are kept as written.
The two lines print 3.1 and 3.10 for the same value. A problem that asks for exactly two decimal places wants the second line.
`x = float(input())` reads 3.14159. Both lines below start from this one value.
`round(x, 2)` returns a float rounded to 2 places, 3.14. A float has no memory of how many digits you wanted, so `print` shows 3.14.
`f"{x:.2f}"` returns text with exactly 2 digits after the point: 3.14. It is a string, so the digits are kept as written.
Both lines print 3.14 this time, because 3.14159 already has at least two decimals. The difference shows up when it has fewer.
`x = float(input())` reads 2.0. Both lines below start from this one value.
`round(x, 2)` returns a float rounded to 2 places, 2.0. A float has no memory of how many digits you wanted, so `print` shows 2.0.
`f"{x:.2f}"` returns text with exactly 2 digits after the point: 2.00. It is a string, so the digits are kept as written.
The two lines print 2.0 and 2.00 for the same value. A problem that asks for exactly two decimal places wants the second line.
